log1p.what: Takes the natural log of (1 + x), compressing large values and right-skewed tails while preserving zero values.
log1p.tradeoff: Effectively reduces right skew and outlier influence. Requires all values ≥ 0; negative values cannot be transformed.
log1p.after: Values are on a log scale. Differences between values represent multiplicative changes in the original.

sqrt.what: Takes the square root of each value. A milder compression than log, suitable for moderate right skew.
sqrt.tradeoff: Less aggressive than log1p; useful when log over-corrects. Requires all values ≥ 0.
sqrt.after: Values are on a square root scale. Units become the square root of the originals, which is less intuitive to interpret.

square.what: Squares each value (x²). Amplifies large positive values and compresses values near zero.
square.tradeoff: Useful for mild left skew. Dramatically amplifies outliers and changes units to the square of the original.
square.after: Values are on a squared scale. The column range and variance will be much larger than before.

yeo_johnson.what: A generalised power transformation that handles negative values. The λ parameter is estimated automatically from the data.
yeo_johnson.tradeoff: Works on any distribution including those with negative values. The transformation is data-specific, making the output harder to interpret directly.
yeo_johnson.after: Values are on a power-transformed scale. The specific transformation depends on the estimated λ - check the fitted value.

box_cox.what: A power transformation similar to Yeo-Johnson but requiring strictly positive values. The λ parameter is estimated automatically.
box_cox.tradeoff: Often achieves better normality than Yeo-Johnson when applicable. Fails on zero or negative values.
box_cox.after: Values are on a power-transformed scale determined by the estimated λ parameter.

winsorize.what: Clips extreme values at specified percentile bounds (e.g., 1st/99th). Extreme values are replaced with the boundary value, not removed.
winsorize.tradeoff: Reduces outlier influence while keeping all rows. Does not reshape the distribution - only truncates the tails. Column retains its original scale.
winsorize.after: The distribution shape is mostly preserved but extreme values are capped. The column range becomes bounded by the chosen percentiles.

reflect_then_log.what: Reflects a left-skewed distribution by subtracting each value from the maximum, then applies log1p to the reflected values.
reflect_then_log.tradeoff: Allows log transformation on left-skewed data where direct log would worsen skew. The reflection reverses the direction of the variable, which changes interpretation.
reflect_then_log.after: Values represent the log of the distance from the original maximum. The direction of the variable is reversed - higher original values become lower transformed values.

gmm_cluster_indicator.what: Fits a Gaussian Mixture Model to the column and adds binary indicators for each detected component - essentially flagging which sub-population each row belongs to.
gmm_cluster_indicator.tradeoff: Useful for bimodal or multimodal columns where the mixture structure carries signal. Adds multiple columns to the dataset. The number of components requires tuning.
gmm_cluster_indicator.after: Adds N binary columns (one per component). The original column may be retained or dropped depending on context.

monitor.what: Keep the column but flag it for active monitoring - track its distribution over time and set up drift alerts rather than transforming it now.
monitor.tradeoff: Preserves all information while acknowledging the issue. Requires infrastructure to monitor distributions in production. Does not address the underlying skew or variance issue.
monitor.after: No immediate change to the column. Set up distribution tracking using a monitoring tool and define alert thresholds.

segment.what: Analyse or model different segments of the data separately, rather than treating the full column as a single distribution.
segment.tradeoff: Can reveal segment-specific patterns that a single model would average over. Requires enough data in each segment to model reliably. Increases complexity.
segment.after: Dataset is split by segment for separate analysis or model training.

use_tree_model.what: Use a tree-based model (e.g. Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM) that is invariant to monotonic transformations of features.
use_tree_model.tradeoff: Eliminates the need to transform the column entirely - tree splits are order-based, not magnitude-based. Trades model flexibility for skew robustness. Linear models, SVMs, and neural nets still benefit from transformation.
use_tree_model.after: No column change required. The model handles skew natively through its split-finding mechanism.

one_hot.what: Creates a separate binary (0/1) indicator column for each unique category value.
one_hot.tradeoff: Simple and universally compatible. Best for low-cardinality columns (< ~15 categories). High-cardinality columns produce too many columns and can cause the curse of dimensionality.
one_hot.after: Each original category becomes its own column. The original column is replaced by N binary columns where N is the number of unique values (minus one if drop_first is used).

bucket_rare_values.what: Groups infrequent category values below a count or proportion threshold into a single "other" bucket before encoding.
bucket_rare_values.tradeoff: Reduces effective cardinality and prevents rare categories from producing unreliable target encoding estimates. Some information about rare categories is lost by merging them.
bucket_rare_values.after: The column still needs a subsequent encoding step. Rare categories are now a single "other" group, which may mix unrelated values.

class_weight.what: Pass class weights to the model so minority classes are penalised more heavily during training, compensating for imbalance.
class_weight.tradeoff: Simple to implement (most sklearn estimators support class_weight="balanced"). Does not change the data - only changes the loss function. May not fully correct severe imbalance.
class_weight.after: No change to the column. The model applies higher penalty for misclassifying the minority class.

stratified_split.what: Use stratified train/test splitting to ensure class proportions are preserved in both the training and test sets.
stratified_split.tradeoff: Simple and always recommended for imbalanced targets. Does not change the data or the model - only the splitting strategy. Essential to avoid train/test distribution mismatch.
stratified_split.after: Both train and test sets reflect the original class distribution. Use stratify=y in sklearn train_test_split.

drop.what: Removes the column entirely from the dataset.
drop.tradeoff: Simple and always valid. Appropriate when missingness is too high to impute reliably, or when the column carries no signal. Permanently loses any information the column contained.
drop.after: The column is absent from the dataset. Any downstream steps that reference it by name will need updating.

add_indicator.what: Adds a binary column (0/1) indicating which rows had a missing value, alongside imputation of the original.
add_indicator.tradeoff: Preserves the information that a value was missing, which can itself be a predictive signal. Adds a column to the dataset. Must be combined with another imputation strategy for the original column.
add_indicator.after: A new binary column captures the missingness pattern. The original column is imputed separately. The model can learn from both the imputed value and whether the value was originally present.

forward_fill.what: Propagates the last known value forward to fill subsequent missing entries. Used for time-ordered or sequential data.
forward_fill.tradeoff: Appropriate when data has temporal structure and adjacent values are likely similar. Inappropriate for non-sequential data or when gaps represent genuinely missing information rather than a continuation.
forward_fill.after: Missing rows receive the value of the most recent non-missing row. Assumes temporal continuity within each series.

investigate.what: Manually examine the column origin, data pipeline, and semantics before taking action.
investigate.tradeoff: Required before dropping or retaining a flagged column - automated detection cannot determine intent. Takes time but prevents incorrect decisions.
investigate.after: Understanding the data provenance determines whether the column is safe to use, should be dropped, or needs re-engineering.

replace_with_nan.what: Replaces sentinel or placeholder values (e.g., -999, 0, "N/A") with actual null values so they are treated as missing rather than as a data point.
replace_with_nan.tradeoff: Essential when placeholder values are present - leaving them in treats them as real data. Increases the apparent missingness rate, which may require follow-up imputation.
replace_with_nan.after: Placeholder values are now null. Apply a missingness strategy afterward.

bin.what: Converts a continuous column into discrete buckets (e.g., deciles or domain-defined ranges).
bin.tradeoff: Can extract signal from near-constant columns where crossing a threshold is meaningful, even if the raw value has near-zero variance. Loses granularity and introduces an arbitrary binning choice.
bin.after: Column becomes categorical with a small number of levels. Apply an encoding step afterward.

robust_scaler.what: Scales each value by subtracting the median and dividing by the interquartile range (IQR), rather than using mean and standard deviation.
robust_scaler.tradeoff: More robust to outliers than standard scaling (StandardScaler) because it uses median and IQR instead of mean and std. Does not bound the output range - extreme outliers still produce extreme scaled values.
robust_scaler.after: Values are centred around 0 (median becomes 0) with the IQR spanning roughly -0.5 to +0.5. Outliers remain but are less dominant.

quantile.what: Divides the column into equal-frequency (quantile) bins, assigning each row to a rank-based bucket rather than a value range.
quantile.tradeoff: Eliminates outlier influence entirely by converting to ranks. Loses the original numeric information - the model sees bins, not values. Bin labels are arbitrary.
quantile.after: Column becomes categorical with a fixed number of buckets. Apply an encoding step afterward.

target_encoding.what: Replaces each category with the mean of the target variable for rows in that category.
target_encoding.tradeoff: Very effective for high-cardinality columns. Must be applied within cross-validation folds to prevent target leakage - applying it to the full dataset before splitting inflates model performance.
target_encoding.after: Column becomes numeric. Similar categories by target rate will have similar encoded values. Rare categories may have noisy estimates.

target.what: Replaces each category with the mean of the target variable for rows in that category.
target.tradeoff: Very effective for high-cardinality columns. Must be applied within cross-validation folds to prevent target leakage - applying it to the full dataset before splitting inflates model performance.
target.after: Column becomes numeric. Similar categories by target rate will have similar encoded values. Rare categories may have noisy estimates.

frequency_encoding.what: Replaces each category with the proportion of rows it appears in across the dataset.
frequency_encoding.tradeoff: No target variable needed. Captures relative frequency as a signal. Does not encode the relationship to the target - common and rare categories are distinguishable, but ordering by frequency may not reflect predictive importance.
frequency_encoding.after: Column becomes numeric (0–1 scale). Frequent categories get large values; rare ones get small values. Categories with equal frequency become indistinguishable.

frequency.what: Replaces each category with the proportion of rows it appears in across the dataset.
frequency.tradeoff: No target variable needed. Captures relative frequency as a signal. Does not encode the relationship to the target - common and rare categories are distinguishable, but ordering by frequency may not reflect predictive importance.
frequency.after: Column becomes numeric (0–1 scale). Frequent categories get large values; rare ones get small values. Categories with equal frequency become indistinguishable.

balanced.what: Pass class weights to the model so minority classes are penalised more heavily during training, compensating for imbalance.
balanced.tradeoff: Simple to implement (most sklearn estimators support class_weight="balanced"). Does not change the data - only changes the loss function. May not fully correct severe imbalance.
balanced.after: No change to the column. The model applies higher penalty for misclassifying the minority class.

oversample_minority.what: Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique. Generates synthetic samples for the minority class by interpolating between existing minority samples.
oversample_minority.tradeoff: More effective than random oversampling at avoiding exact duplicates. Must be applied only to the training fold - never to validation or test data. Can introduce noisy samples near class boundaries.
oversample_minority.after: Training set gains synthetic minority class rows. Class distribution becomes more balanced. Apply within cross-validation folds.

model_based.what: Trains a predictive model on the non-missing rows to predict the missing values from other columns.
model_based.tradeoff: Produces the most statistically plausible imputations by leveraging relationships between columns. Computationally expensive and requires careful cross-validation to avoid leakage.
model_based.after: Missing values are replaced with model-predicted estimates. Imputed values reflect patterns learned from the full observed dataset.

iterative.what: Trains a predictive model on the non-missing rows to predict the missing values from other columns.
iterative.tradeoff: Produces the most statistically plausible imputations by leveraging relationships between columns. Computationally expensive and requires careful cross-validation to avoid leakage.
iterative.after: Missing values are replaced with model-predicted estimates. Imputed values reflect patterns learned from the full observed dataset.

mean.what: Replaces missing values with the mean of the non-missing values.
mean.tradeoff: Fast and simple, and suited to roughly symmetric columns. Sensitive to outliers, and every imputed row gets the same value, so variance shrinks.
mean.after: Missing rows all receive the mean. The distribution becomes slightly more concentrated around the centre.

mode.what: Replaces missing values with the most frequent value.
mode.tradeoff: The usual choice for categorical and boolean columns. Over-represents the most common value and ignores the other columns.
mode.after: Missing rows all receive the most frequent value; its share of the column grows.

constant_missing.what: Fills missing values with an explicit placeholder such as "missing", so absence becomes a category of its own.
constant_missing.tradeoff: Keeps the fact that a value was absent, which is often informative, and needs no assumption about the missing values. The placeholder must not collide with a real value.
constant_missing.after: The column has one more level. Encode it afterwards like any other categorical column.

binary.what: Writes each category as a binary code spread over a few 0/1 columns (about log2 of the number of levels).
binary.tradeoff: Far fewer columns than one-hot for a medium number of levels. The codes have no meaning, so linear models can read structure into them that is not there.
binary.after: The column becomes about log2(levels) binary columns.

equal_width.what: Cuts the value range into bins of equal width.
equal_width.tradeoff: Easy to read and keeps the shape of the distribution. Bins at a skewed or crowded column's tails hold few rows, so quantile bins are the safer choice there.
equal_width.after: The column becomes categorical with a fixed number of levels. Encode it afterwards.

impute:median.what: Replaces missing values with the median of the non-missing values.
impute:median.tradeoff: More robust to outliers and skewed distributions than mean imputation. Does not preserve variance.
impute:median.after: Missing rows all receive the same value (the median). Works well when the distribution is skewed or has outliers.

winsorize:iqr_fences.what: Clips extreme values at specified percentile bounds (e.g., 1st/99th). Extreme values are replaced with the boundary value, not removed.
winsorize:iqr_fences.tradeoff: Reduces outlier influence while keeping all rows. Does not reshape the distribution - only truncates the tails. Column retains its original scale.
winsorize:iqr_fences.after: The distribution shape is mostly preserved but extreme values are capped. The column range becomes bounded by the chosen percentiles.

winsorize:clip_to_bounds.what: Clips extreme values at specified percentile bounds (e.g., 1st/99th). Extreme values are replaced with the boundary value, not removed.
winsorize:clip_to_bounds.tradeoff: Reduces outlier influence while keeping all rows. Does not reshape the distribution - only truncates the tails. Column retains its original scale.
winsorize:clip_to_bounds.after: The distribution shape is mostly preserved but extreme values are capped. The column range becomes bounded by the chosen percentiles.

add_indicator:is_missing.what: Adds a binary column (0/1) indicating which rows had a missing value, alongside imputation of the original.
add_indicator:is_missing.tradeoff: Preserves the information that a value was missing, which can itself be a predictive signal. Adds a column to the dataset. Must be combined with another imputation strategy for the original column.
add_indicator:is_missing.after: A new binary column captures the missingness pattern. The original column is imputed separately. The model can learn from both the imputed value and whether the value was originally present.
